issue: PMAT-600 (forjar#600) — a `state: file` check_script was `test -f`, so `apply --refresh` (re-apply only what fails) certified a file holding the wrong bytes through both doors: refresh seeding with no lock entry, and a lock entry, where one run on intel printed `drift: … pv.pin content changed` and then `0 converged`, leaving a fleet pin at 0.65.2 under a declaration of 0.68.2 (2026-09-21 10:41Z). The check now asserts existence, the sha256 of the declared bytes, an octal mode and owner/group where declared.

quorum.kill_rule: nothing was dismissed; no lane raised a finding. Both refutations came from the author's own tests before the quorum: forjar's I8 gate refusing the inline form, and the issue's mechanism naming one door of two.
refuted_claims: R1: the first content assertion put `||` inside `[ "$(…)" = x ]`; bashrs SC2107 read it as `[ a || b ]` at Error and the I8 gate refused every file check (20+ lib tests). Now assign-then-test; bashrs#366 fixed in bashrs#367.
R2: the issue named refresh seeding (unlocked resources) as the mechanism; a locked resource went through the same check. The fix is in check_script, which both doors consult.

crux.verdict: Shipped behaviour change: a file check now fails on stale content or mode, so `apply --refresh` writes it. CHANGELOG [Unreleased] carries it. Every major configuration tool decides a managed file's convergence by content and attributes, never by existence alone.
systems: Ansible copy/template: compares the checksum of the destination with the source before writing, and reports changed only when they differ; mode/owner are compared separately [X]
Puppet file resource: content is compared by checksum (md5 by default, sha256 selectable), and mode/owner/group are separate properties each reported on change [X]
Chef file/template: a sha256 checksum of the current file against the rendered content decides whether the resource updates; mode/owner/group are checked as attributes [X]
